claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a high-temperature BCC state.
Localized solute partitioning during cooling and thermal exposure promotes heterogeneous nucleation of secondary phases.
Formation of secondary phases through heterogeneous nucleation destabilizes the high-temperature BCC structure.
Differential elemental diffusion rates create local chemical fluctuations that serve as nucleation sites for phase transformations.
Larger atomic species diffuse more slowly than the faster-diffusing species relevant to this alloy.
Rapid quenching arrests diffusion and suppresses solute partitioning.
Rapidly quenching this alloy from its high-temperature BCC state retains a homogeneous, single-phase BCC structure.
Slower cooling followed by an isothermal hold permits sufficient diffusion for local solute partitioning.
Solute-rich and solute-lean regions act as nucleation sites for secondary phases.
Differential diffusion during slow cooling and isothermal holding causes certain elements to cluster.
Elemental clustering reduces the chemical homogeneity of the BCC matrix.
Local compositional fluctuations lower the nucleation barrier for secondary-phase formation or ordering transitions.
Compared with the rapidly quenched baseline, the slowly cooled and thermally exposed sample will develop secondary phases.
The predicted secondary phases will produce new X-ray diffraction peaks and distinct microscopy features.
The phase change will be significant if diffusion is sufficiently activated.
The proposed mechanism applies only in a temperature and cooling-rate window that permits appreciable differential diffusion and partitioning.
The mechanism should not operate after sufficiently rapid quenching or at temperatures where atomic mobility is negligible.
A lack of both increased local partitioning and secondary-phase formation in the slowly cooled and held samples relative to the quenched control would falsify the proposed mechanism.
Comparable phase transformations regardless of cooling rate and thermal exposure would falsify the claimed causal role of differential diffusion and partitioning.
